    📘 Getting Started with CrystalPilot▾
    Turn raw diffraction images → measured intensities with a known space group and unit cell, ready for structure determination.
    1
    Create or select a project in the sidebar (left panel). Each project is a processing directory.
    2
    Set up parameters — load an existing XDS.INP from your beamline (click ⟳ Load from XDS.INP). If none is available, use ⚡ Generate from images to read geometry from data files.
    3
    Run ▶ to IDXREF to index the crystal. Check that indexing worked (high indexed %, reasonable unit cell).
    4
    Run ▶ Integrate & Correct to process all frames. Inspect Key Metrics for Rmeas, CC½, and I/σ.
    💡 Switch to Tutorial mode in the sidebar to see 📘 hints throughout the interface explaining each section.
    XDS: Kabsch, W. (2010) Acta Cryst. D66, 125–132. doi:10.1107/S0907444909047337 · Download: xds.mr.mpg.de
    Pipeline click step to view LP · ▶ to run
    📘 The XDS pipelineclick to read▸
    processes your diffraction images in eight steps. XYCORR corrects for spatial distortions in the detector. INIT measures the background and detector gain. COLSPOT finds strong diffraction spots across a subset of frames. IDXREF determines the crystal's unit cell and orientation by fitting a lattice to those spot positions — this is the critical indexing step. DEFPIX defines the trusted region of the detector, excluding areas like the beamstop shadow, ice rings, and detector edges that would corrupt intensity measurements. XPLAN (optional) estimates data completeness for collection strategy. INTEGRATE measures each reflection's intensity by 3D profile fitting across all frames — the most computationally intensive step. CORRECT scales the data, determines the space group, reports merging statistics (Rmeas, CC1/2, I/σ), and produces the final reflection file (XDS_ASCII.HKL) — this is where you assess data quality and decide the resolution cutoff. Steps turn green when complete — click one to inspect its log file.
    Run Controls
    ⟳ Running...
    📘 Getting started:click to read▸
    For a first run, you can leave the run folder blank (it defaults to your project folder). Click ▶ to IDXREF to run through indexing — this processes frames through XYCORR → INIT → COLSPOT → IDXREF and lets you check that the crystal indexes correctly before committing to full integration. If indexing looks good (high indexed %, σ(spot) near 1 pixel, reasonable unit cell), run ▶ Integrate & Correct to process all frames and produce final statistics. Check the Key Metrics after each run to assess quality.
    📘 Locating your data — the first step.click to read▸
    Before processing, CrystalPilot needs to know where your diffraction images are and what parameters to use. You can set up parameters in several ways: ① Import from an existing XDS.INP — if you already have one (e.g. from a beamline auto-processing pipeline like autoPROC, xia2, or EDNA, or from a previous XDS run), click ⟳ Load from XDS.INP to import from the project folder, or 📂 Load from other XDS.INP… to browse to one in another directory. ② Generate from images — set the NAME_TEMPLATE_OF_DATA_FRAMES path (type it directly, or use 📂 to browse for an image file — the filename is auto-converted to an XDS template), then click ⚡ Generate from images to read detector geometry, wavelength, oscillation range, and other parameters from the image headers. ③ Manual entry — you can always fill in or adjust any parameter field directly in the Key Parameters tab. All approaches can be combined: import or generate first, then review and edit as needed. ⚡ Generate from images automatically saves to disk. When loading from another directory or entering parameters manually, press 💾 Save Parameters to write the XDS.INP file before running.

    Experimental Parameters
    
                                    
    📘 These describe your experiment.click to read▸
    The wavelength (in Å) must be on the order of interatomic distances for diffraction to occur — typical synchrotron values are 0.9–1.1 Å. Oscillation range is the rotation per frame; smaller values (0.1–0.2°) give finer sampling of reciprocal space but more frames. Detector distance controls the maximum resolution recorded: shorter distance captures higher-angle (higher-resolution) reflections, but spots may overlap if the crystal has a large unit cell. These values are usually read from the image header via ⚡ Generate from images.
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
    
                                            
                                            
                                        
    
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        No XDS.INP? Set the template above, then click Generate.
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                
    
                                
    
                                    
    Detector Parameters
    
                                    
    📘 Detector geometry matters.click to read▸
    ORGX/ORGY define the direct beam position on the detector (in pixels) — an inaccurate beam center is the most common cause of indexing failure. QX/QY are pixel sizes (mm), needed to convert pixel positions to scattering angles. NX/NY give the detector dimensions. OVERLOAD is the maximum trusted pixel value — pixels above this are excluded as saturated. These are usually set correctly by ⚡ Generate from images or imported from an existing XDS.INP, but if indexing fails, check ORGX/ORGY first.

    Indexing Parameters
    
                                    
    📘 Indexing = finding the crystal lattice.click to read▸
    Set SPACE_GROUP_NUMBER to 0 to let XDS determine the lattice automatically — this is recommended for a first pass. IDXREF will report quality-of-fit values for 14 Bravais lattice types (44 lattice characters); CORRECT later determines the space group by testing all compatible symmetry operations. The unit cell (a, b, c, α, β, γ) describes the repeating box of your crystal. DATA_RANGE sets which frames to process; SPOT_RANGE selects frames for spot-finding — using frames ~90° apart in rotation helps indexing by sampling more of reciprocal space. FRIEDEL'S_LAW=TRUE means Bijvoet pairs are treated as equivalent (no anomalous signal); set to FALSE for SAD/MAD experiments.

    Corrections
    
                                    
    📘 Correcting systematic effects.click to read▸
    Raw diffraction intensities are affected by several physical factors. Decay accounts for radiation damage over time. Absorption corrects for the varying path length of X-rays through the crystal at different orientations. Modulation handles detector response non-uniformity. The default ALL applies all three corrections — you rarely need to change this for routine processing.
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                
    
                                
    
                                    
    Reporting
    
                                    
    📘 Resolution limits.click to read▸
    Resolution in crystallography is measured in Ångströms (Å) — smaller numbers mean higher resolution. INCLUDE_RESOLUTION_RANGE sets the range of data to use, e.g. 50.0 to 2.0 Å. The high-resolution cutoff is one of the most important decisions in data processing. Modern practice recommends using CC1/2 (the correlation between random half-datasets) rather than I/σ alone to determine where useful signal ends (Karplus & Diederichs, 2012).

    📘 Reading log files is essential.click to read▸
    Every XDS step writes a .LP file with detailed output. Key things to check: In IDXREF.LP, look at the standard deviation of spot position (~1 pixel is good) and the subtree table (the first subtree should dominate). In CORRECT.LP, look at the resolution shell table for Rmeas (agreement between symmetry-equivalent reflections), I/σ (signal-to-noise), and CC1/2 (correlation between random half-datasets). Use Key Metrics below to see these extracted into charts.

    📘 Inspecting diffraction images.click to read▸
    Each frame is a snapshot of the diffraction pattern at one rotation angle. Well-diffracting crystals show spots extending to the edge of the detector (high resolution). Look for: clean spots with low background (good crystal), ice rings (powder rings from frozen solvent — the strongest appear near ~3.9, ~3.7, and ~3.4 Å resolution), split spots (multiple lattices or high mosaicity), and how far spots extend (resolution limit). Enable Resolution Rings to see Å markers, and Spot Overlay to compare predicted vs. observed spots after indexing.

    Quick GuideCrystalPilot v0.6.8
    
                
    
                
    XDS Documentation: xds.mr.mpg.de/html_doc/XDS.html — the official reference for all XDS parameters and methods (W. Kabsch, MPI Heidelberg). The Docs tab next to this one is the complete CrystalPilot manual.
    1 · Install and start
    Linux: bash install-linux.sh next to the application file, then crystalpilot. Windows: CrystalPilot-Setup.bat once, then the desktop shortcut. The interface opens at http://127.0.0.1:8000. On the first start the Environment screen tells you what was found (XDS, neggia for Eiger data, CCP4, Python packages) and how to fix anything missing; it is always reachable from the About panel.
    2 · Create or select a project
    In the sidebar type a name and click ＋ Create Project, or click an existing one. A project is a folder that holds your input files and results; Open folder shows it in your file manager (under Windows also as P:\Projects\...).
    3 · Set up XDS.INP
    Generate from images reads geometry, wavelength, oscillation and frame count from the frame headers (Eiger master files included, with the neggia LIB= line); Load from XDS.INP or Load from other XDS.INP… imports an existing file; or type values in the Key Parameters form. Toggles mark a keyword active or commented. From IDXREF fills cell and space group from the lattice table once IDXREF has run. Edit exotic keywords in the Full Input File tab.
    4 · Run
    ▶ to IDXREF first, then ▶ Integrate & Correct; ⚡ CORRECT Only after changing symmetry or resolution; GXPARM Re-integrate for a second pass with refined geometry. Choose overwrite or numbered sub-folders in the run-folder field. ⏹ Stop ends the run and its helper processes. If indexing fails, the Auto-Index card tries spot ranges and thresholds for you.
    5 · Inspect
    Click a green step for its log; Key Metrics gives tables and charts (lattice table, per-frame scale and mosaicity, shell statistics, Wilson plot, moments, aliens, anomalous signal, cut-off estimates with apply buttons). Run History compares the last runs, Compare… an uploaded log. The Matthews calculator sits under the CORRECT metrics. Export parsed data as CSV.
    6 · Frame Viewer
    Load a frame or the XDS template (or From XDS.INP), step through the series, adjust contrast and zoom, open the magnifier with Mag, show resolution rings, ice rings and the SPOT.XDS overlay, save the view as PNG. The path is remembered per project; Recent lists the last five.
    7 · XSCALE
    Add the XDS_ASCII.HKL files (Auto-detect), Autofill from CORRECT.LP for symmetry and resolution, set Friedel's law and merge mode, save (Update keeps the file, Save new starts clean; both write a valid XSCALE layout) and run. The LP viewer shows the statistics and cut-off estimates for the merged data.
    8 · Space group and independent scaling
    POINTLESS determines the Laue and space group and can apply it to XDS.INP and re-run CORRECT. AIMLESS scales and merges independently, with CTRUNCATE amplitudes and twinning tests, and compares its statistics with XDS. Both need CCP4.
    9 · Frame quality
    ΔCC½ runs XDSCC12 to find frames that harm the data; accept the suggested exclusions and re-run CORRECT with one click.
    10 · Convert
    XDSCONV writes CCP4 / MTZ (with f2mtz and cad when CCP4 is present, or with gemmi otherwise), SHELX or XtalView files with free-R flags.
    11 · AutoPilot
    A wizard: drop the folders, check which beamline XDS.INP each data set imports, choose the cut-offs, the reprocessing (GXPARM re-integration, ΔCC½) and what to do with the space group and failed indexing, review, start. Every data set is processed unattended with error recovery, XSCALE and MTZ output; compare them in one table and merge the best.
    12 · Checks with gemmi
    Merging statistics and completeness computed independently, lattice symmetry hints, anomalous scattering factors, a deposition CIF and a polarization check.
    13 · Table 1
    The Statistics tab builds a publication Table 1 from XSCALE.LP or CORRECT.LP; copy as TSV or LaTeX, or export a .csv.
    14 · Tips
    • Work mode (Tutorial / Normal / Advanced / Expert) controls how much is shown; the cut-off preference sets the criterion autofill uses.
    • Everything reads and writes in the folder of the last run; the status line under the run-folder field shows it.
    • The server answers only the browser tab that opened it; scripts need the token printed at start (X-CrystalPilot-Token). --host 0.0.0.0 opens it to the network, --restrict-browse confines the file browser.
    • Under Windows keep large Eiger data in the projects folder; the Windows drives are under /mnt/c, /mnt/z…
    • Parameter references: XDS.INP · XSCALE.INP · XDSCONV.INP.
    
                
    
                
    
                
    

                
                
    

                    
                    
    
                    
    XDS/XSCALE: Kabsch, W. (2010) Acta Cryst. D66, 125–132. doi:10.1107/S0907444909047337 · Download: xds.mr.mpg.de
    

                    
    📘 XSCALE scales and merges datasets.click to read▸
    After integration by XDS, each dataset produces an XDS_ASCII.HKL file containing unmerged reflection intensities. XSCALE puts multiple datasets (or a single one) on a common scale, applies corrections for radiation damage and absorption, and merges symmetry-equivalent reflections. This is where you decide: merge with Friedel's law TRUE (native data, no anomalous signal) or FALSE (anomalous data, keeping Bijvoet pairs separate for SAD/MAD phasing).

    Autofill from CORRECT.LP
    
                                        
    📘 Autofill transfers key results from CORRECT to XSCALE.click to read▸
    Clicking 🔄 Autofill from CORRECT.LP reads the space group, unit cell constants, and resolution statistics from your latest CORRECT.LP and populates the fields below automatically. This saves you from manually copying numbers between steps. Resolution cutoff criterion: you choose how aggressively to cut data — I/σ ≈ 2.0 is the traditional conservative cutoff (where signal-to-noise becomes marginal); R-obs ≈ 55% uses the merging R-factor threshold; CC½ ≈ 50% is a commonly used intermediate threshold where the half-dataset correlation is still meaningful; CC½ signif. keeps data to the last shell where the half-dataset correlation is statistically significant (Karplus & Diederichs, 2012) — this is typically the most generous cutoff and often gives the best maps, as weak high-resolution data still contributes useful phase information. The autofill interpolates your CORRECT statistics to find the exact resolution where your chosen criterion is met, and sets INCLUDE_RESOLUTION_RANGE accordingly.

                    📖 XSCALE Parameter Reference
                
    

                
    

                
                
    
                    
    📘 Table 1 is the standard summary tableclick to read▸
    included in crystallography publications. It reports space group, unit cell, resolution, completeness, redundancy (multiplicity), Rmeas, CC1/2, and I/σ — both overall and for the highest resolution shell (in parentheses). Reviewers and readers use these numbers to judge data quality. High completeness (>95%), reasonable Rmeas, and significant CC1/2 in the outer shell indicate a well-collected and well-processed dataset.

                            POINTLESS — Space Group Determination
                            
                        
    
                        
    
                            
    Determines the correct Laue group and space group by scoring symmetry operators against your unmerged reflection data (XDS_ASCII.HKL). Run this after CORRECT if the space group assignment is uncertain, if you observe unexplained systematic absences, or whenever you want a rigorous, independent confirmation before proceeding to scaling. Requires CCP4.
    

                            
    Reference: Evans, P. R. (2011) Acta Cryst. D67, 282–292. doi:10.1107/S090744491003982X  |  Evans, P. (2006) Acta Cryst. D62, 72–82. doi:10.1107/S0907444905036693
    
                            
    
                            
    CCP4 suite: Agirre, J. et al. (2023) Acta Cryst. D79, 449–461. doi:10.1107/S2059798323003595 · Download: www.ccp4.ac.uk/download
    

                            
    📘 POINTLESS determines the Laue group and space group.click to read▸
    While XDS CORRECT makes an initial space group assignment, POINTLESS (Phil Evans, CCP4) performs a more rigorous analysis by scoring all possible symmetry operators against the diffraction data and examining systematic absences. It is the standard tool for definitive space group determination in macromolecular crystallography. POINTLESS reads your unmerged XDS_ASCII.HKL directly and outputs a reindexed MTZ file ready for scaling with AIMLESS. Use CHIRALITY CHIRAL for proteins (65 space groups) and NONCHIRAL for small molecules (230 space groups). The SYMMETRY-BASED setting is recommended for XDS users to avoid axis-labeling ambiguities.

                            ΔCC½ — Frame Quality Analysis
                            
                        
    
                        
    
                            
    Identifies which frames are hurting your data by computing per-frame ΔCC½ — the change in overall CC½ when each frame is removed. Negative values indicate frames that reduce data quality (radiation damage, ice hits, etc.). Requires XDSCC12 (Kay Diederichs, Uni Konstanz) and a completed CORRECT step.
    

                            
    Reference: Assmann, G., Brehm, W. & Diederichs, K. (2016) J. Appl. Cryst. 49, 1021–1028. doi:10.1107/S1600576716005471
    
                            
    

                            
    📘 ΔCC½ measures each frame's contribution to data quality.click to read▸
    XDSCC12 implements the leave-one-out method from Assmann, Brehm & Diederichs (2016) J. Appl. Cryst. 49, 1021–1028. For each batch of frames, it calculates ΔCC½ = CC½(with) − CC½(without). Positive values mean the frame improves the data; negative values mean it hurts. The black line shows the overall contribution; colored lines show per-resolution-shell contributions (blue=low res → red=high res). Frames with strongly negative ΔCC½ at high resolution are prime candidates for exclusion via EXCLUDE_DATA_RANGE. The -t option batches fine-sliced frames (e.g. 0.1°) into wider groups (typically 1°) for reliable statistics.
    

                            
                            
    
                                
    Options
    
                                
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                
    
                                
    
                                    
                                    
    
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                    
    
                                
    
                            
    

                            
                            
    💡 Tip: For meaningful results, ensure INCLUDE_RESOLUTION_RANGE is set to a reasonable resolution cutoff and CORRECT has been run before launching ΔCC½ analysis. If the cutoff is too generous, noisy high-resolution shells will make most frames appear negative.

                            AIMLESS — Scale & Merge
                            
                        
    
                        
    
                            
    Runs the full CCP4 scaling pipeline: POINTLESS (reindex) → AIMLESS (scale, merge, SD correction, outlier rejection) → CTRUNCATE (French-Wilson amplitudes, twinning tests). Produces a publication-ready MTZ file. Requires CCP4.
    

                            
    References: Evans, P.R. & Murshudov, G.N. (2013) Acta Cryst. D69, 1204-1214. doi:10.1107/S0907444913000061 · Evans, P.R. (2006) Acta Cryst. D62, 72-82.
    

                            
    

                            
    📚 AIMLESS scales and merges symmetry-related reflections.click to read▸
    While XDS CORRECT provides initial scaling, AIMLESS (Phil Evans, CCP4) performs a more sophisticated empirical error model (SD correction), robust outlier rejection, and produces detailed diagnostics including radiation damage analysis (B-factor vs. batch), anisotropy analysis, and run-pair correlations. It is the community-standard program for producing publication-ready merged data. CTRUNCATE then converts intensities to amplitudes using the French-Wilson algorithm and performs twinning tests (L-test, H-test) and anisotropy correction. The pipeline reads XDS_ASCII.HKL via POINTLESS (which reindexes and sorts) and produces a final MTZ with F, SIGF, IMEAN, SIGIMEAN columns ready for molecular replacement or phasing.

    📘 XDSCONV converts reflection filesclick to read▸
    from XDS format into formats used by downstream programs. Common targets: CCP4/MTZ (for refinement with REFMAC, Phenix, or molecular replacement with Phaser), SHELX (for small-molecule or substructure determination), CNS (for simulated annealing). If CCP4 is installed, CrystalPilot automatically runs f2mtz and cad to produce a ready-to-use MTZ file with both intensities and structure factor amplitudes.

    CCP4: Agirre, J. et al. (2023) Acta Cryst. D79, 449–461. doi:10.1107/S2059798323003595 · Download: www.ccp4.ac.uk/download

    🚀 AutoPilot
    
                    
    
                        Set it up once, for one data set or many: the folders, the XDS.INP to start from, the cut-offs, the reprocessing and what to do when indexing fails.
                        Nothing runs until you press Start on the last step. Every data set becomes a project of its own and is processed one after the other;
                        close the page if you like — the run carries on and this tab picks it up again.

A browser never tells a web page where a dragged folder is, so AutoPilot finds it by its name and its files — in recently used folders, the projects folder, the home folder and the drives. If it is not found, paste the path (Explorer: Shift + right-click → Copy as path) or use Browse.
